summary: For ages 7–8, teach the flowering-plant life cycle as a repeating cycle (flower → pollination → seed formation → dispersal → germination → new plant) and anchor dispersal in a STRUCTURE→FUNCTION idea: a seed's shape reveals how it travels. Keep pollination simple and mechanistic (pollen is carried from flower to flower, by insects or wind, so a seed can form); reserve anther/stigma anatomy for older learners. Make the PURPOSE of dispersal explicit — seeds spread away so offspring don't compete with the parent for light, water and space. The discriminating skill is predicting a seed's dispersal method from its shape with a reason (e.g. 'wings, so the wind spins it far from the parent').
misconceptions: Confusing pollination with seed dispersal — treating them as the same 'spreading' step, rather than pollination (making the seed) then dispersal (moving the finished seed).
Thinking pollination is only done by bees — missing wind pollination and other carriers.
Believing seeds are dispersed so they 'find nice soil', rather than to escape competition with the parent for light/water/space.
Thinking the parent plant 'decides' or actively throws all its seeds, missing that most mechanisms are passive (wind, hitching a ride, floating).
Assuming the seed's shape is decorative/random rather than functional for how it travels.
Conflating pollen with seeds — thinking pollen itself grows into the new plant.

activities.title: Seed-launch test: match shape to travel method
steps: Gather a set of real, differently-shaped seeds where you can — a winged sycamore key, a spiky burr, a fluffy dandelion parachute, a fruit that floats (e.g. a coconut, which is heavy but floats because of its air-filled, fibrous husk), and a poppy-style shaker pod; use pictures only to supplement, because the hands-on tests below need real specimens.
For each seed, choose how to send it off — turn up a breeze (a fan or blowing), drop it in a tray of water, or brush it past a woolly sock/fur to stand for a passing animal — and send it.

Do the hands-on tests: drop and spin the winged seed, blow the dandelion parachute, press the burr onto wool, float the fruit in water, and shake the dry poppy head to see seeds fall out of the holes at its top.
After each test, state which feature made it travel ('wings spin on the wind', 'hooks grab fur', 'parachute floats', 'air-filled husk floats on water', 'pod shakes seeds out as the stem sways').
For any seed that just drops straight down at the parent's feet, explain out loud why that is a problem for the new seedling.
activities.insight: A seed's shape is functional, not decorative: the shape predicts and explains how the seed travels, and travelling far matters because a seed dropped beside the parent competes with it for light, water and space.

activities.title: Fly the pollinator: make a seed, then close the cycle
steps: Use two pictures or models of the same kind of flower and a bee token (or a cotton-bud 'bee').
Move the bee from one flower to the other, carrying 'pollen' (e.g. a dab of flour or coloured dots) between them.
Say what just happened in your own words: the pollen was MOVED from flower to flower — that is pollination — and only after that can a seed form.
Also show wind pollination by blowing pollen from one flower picture toward another, so bees are not the only carrier.

Pick a real seed to stand for the seed that would form inside a real flower over the following days or weeks, run it through the seed-launch test above, then draw the full circle: flower → pollination → seed forms → dispersal → germination → new flowering plant.
activities.insight: Pollination (moving pollen between flowers) and seed formation are different steps, and they are the reproduction stage of a repeating life cycle that returns to a new plant.

activities.title: Reference and check: cycle order, shape→method, and why disperse
steps: Order the stages of the flowering-plant life cycle into a circle that returns to a new plant.

Pair each seed shape with its dispersal method: winged → spins on wind; hooked burr → grabs animal fur; parachute → floats on wind; fruit with an air-filled husk (e.g. coconut) → floats on water; shaker pod (e.g. poppy) → shakes seeds out as the stem sways; springy pod (e.g. gorse or pea) → bursts and flings seeds out.
Answer and justify: 'Why are seeds spread far from the parent plant?' giving a competition-for-light/water/space reason, not just 'to find soil'.
For one seed of your choice, predict its dispersal method from its shape alone and state the reason before testing it.
activities.insight: The learner can sequence the cycle, link seed shape to travel method, and give the survival reason for dispersal — predicting method from shape with justification.

activities.title: Bagged-flower investigation: does a flower need a pollinator?
steps: Choose a plant that needs insects to carry pollen between flowers to set seed (many flowers, such as peas and tomatoes, can pollinate themselves and would still set seed in a bag). Cover one of its flowers with a fine mesh bag so insects cannot reach it, and leave a matching nearby flower open.
Predict which flower will form seeds and explain WHY before waiting.
After time passes, compare how many seeds (or fruit) each flower set.

Explain the result: the open flower could be visited by insects carrying pollen and the bagged one could not, so if the bagged flower set fewer or no seeds, that suggests this plant needs insects to carry its pollen; if both set seed, discuss whether this plant can pollinate itself.
activities.insight: Seed formation needs pollination; in plants that rely on insects, pollen must be carried to the flower by a visitor before seeds can form.

checkQuestion: A bee lands on a flower, then flies to another flower. Later that first flower makes seeds inside a fruit, and the seeds end up carried far away from the parent plant. Walk me through what the bee did and what happened next — and explain WHY it helps the plant for its seeds to travel far away rather than drop straight down.
checkAnswer: The bee carried POLLEN from one flower to another — that's pollination; the pollen then joins with the egg (fertilisation) so seeds form; the fruit/seeds are then dispersed (wind, animals, water, or bursting). Seeds travel far so the new plants don't crowd and compete with the parent for light, water and space. Full marks put the stages in order AND give a survival reason for dispersal.
